name: Under-eye chemical peel (TCA/lunch peel)

card.summary: A chemical peel aimed at the thin skin under the eyes to lighten pigment and smooth texture; popular in discussion, thinly studied for this exact site.
card.aka: TCA peel, lunch peel, periorbital peel
card.note: Periocular skin is thin; documented peel risks include pigment change, scarring and prolonged redness.

quick.overview:
An under-eye chemical peel applies an acid solution, such as trichloroacetic acid (TCA), to the lower-eyelid area to remove outer skin layers. People in appearance communities discuss it as a way to address darkness, fine lines and crepey texture under the eyes.

Peels in general are an established dermatology tool for texture and pigment. Published trials specific to peeling the under-eye area are not part of the material reviewed for this entry, so its evidence for dark circles is described here as limited.
quick.mechanism: Peel acids cause a controlled injury to the epidermis and sometimes upper dermis, after which the skin sheds and regenerates. Depth depends on the acid, its strength and how it is applied; TCA is classed as a medium-depth agent.
quick.risks: Reported peel complications include prolonged redness, pigment changes, skin thinning, texture changes, milia and scarring, with higher risk from deeper peels and unsupervised home kits. The skin around the eyes is thin, and peels are performed by clinicians in medical settings. No sources reviewed give a regulatory status specific to this use.

lead: An under-eye chemical peel is the application of an exfoliating acid, most commonly trichloroacetic acid (TCA) in forum discussion, to the skin of the lower eyelids and infraorbital area. The goal described by users is lighter periorbital pigmentation, smoother texture and fewer fine lines. The nickname "lunch peel" refers to the idea of a quick procedure with limited downtime, a term used in cosmetic practice for light peels.

Chemical peeling in general is a long-established cosmetic procedure that removes outer skin layers; light peels are done in clinics and med spas, while medium peels such as TCA are meant to be performed by medical providers [1]. Periorbital hyperpigmentation, the condition most people mean by dark circles, is described as a common trait involving excess melanin that is most prevalent in people aged 16 to 25 [2].

No clinical trials of under-eye TCA peels were identified for this article, so evidence for the specific use is limited. Evidence for peels on other facial sites exists, and general risks of peeling are documented.

paras: Chemical peels are classified by depth. Alpha hydroxy acids such as glycolic and lactic acid are the mildest; salicylic acid is a beta hydroxy acid used for acne; TCA is a medium-depth peel done in offices or outpatient surgical centers and commonly causes a warm or burning sensation; phenol-croton oil peels are the deepest [1]. Peeling is described as reducing fine lines, acne scars and uneven pigment through controlled injury [1].

For the under-eye area, practitioners and forum users typically discuss lower-strength or lighter formulations because the skin there is thin. No sources reviewed for this article specify standard concentrations for this site, and none are given here.

Peels were introduced in the second half of the 19th century by Austrian dermatologist Ferdinand von Hebra, who used agents including phenol and nitric acid for freckles and skin irregularities; phenol-croton oil peels entered mainstream practice in the 1960s [1].

Peel complications described in general include photosensitivity, prolonged redness, pigment changes, milia, skin thinning, texture changes, injury and scarring, particularly with unsupervised home kits [1]. Because periorbital skin is thin and adjacent to the eye, people discussing the procedure often describe it as one for professionals; no published safety data specific to this site were located.

No studies found on under-eye TCA peels for periorbital pigmentation. A registered trial has examined a medium-depth peel on the outer corners of the eyes (lateral canthal wrinkles) with or without pretreatment with botulinum toxin, a different goal from dark circles [3]. Other registry hits returned for the term "peeling" concern retinal surgery and are unrelated.

timeline.event: Ferdinand von Hebra introduces chemical peels in Austria [1].
Phenol-croton oil peel enters mainstream practice [1].

refs.title: Lateral Canthal Rhytides With Medium Depth Chemical Peel With or Without Pretreatment With Botulinum Toxin A
